title: Firecracker Prices May Jump 30–50% This Diwali as Unsold Stock Piles Up
excerpt: Traders are asking sharply more for popular varieties while Sivakasi sits on ₹6,000 crore of unsold stock and courts decide where green crackers can be sold.
body:
• Traders are asking 30–50% more for popular firecrackers this Diwali, Business Standard reported — up from the 15–20% rise we reported on October 13.
  • Sivakasi, India's firecracker capital, is sitting on about ₹6,000 crore of unsold stock; its 2025 production was ₹7,000 crore and roughly 8 lakh workers depend on the industry.
  • Retail prices in Chennai are up about 10% so far, Hindustan Times found — the final Diwali price depends on court rulings on where green crackers can be sold.
  • The Madras High Court allowed green crackers in Delhi on October 10; the Supreme Court reserved its judgment on October 14.

The Diwali firecracker bill is climbing faster than expected. Traders in wholesale hubs are now asking 30–50% more than last year for popular varieties, Business Standard reported — a sharp step up from the 15–20% increase we reported on October 13, when the pressure was coming from Sivakasi's production cuts and labour shortage.

Why the Asking Price Jumped

The new driver is a pile-up at both ends of the trade. Sivakasi's manufacturers are holding an estimated ₹6,000 crore of unsold stock — much of it produced before court decisions narrowed where crackers can legally be sold. The town's 2025 production was worth about ₹7,000 crore, and around 8 lakh workers depend on the industry directly or indirectly. With legal selling windows shrinking, traders who do have stock in permitted markets are pricing it like a scarce good.

At retail, the pass-through has only partly arrived. Hindustan Times reported Chennai prices up about 10% ahead of Diwali, with roughly 1,200 licensed shops at the Island Grounds fair and individual items already dearer: a 10-wala bijili string at ₹70–80 in Bengaluru, sparklers at ₹100 a dozen against ₹70–80 earlier. Whether the wholesale 30–50% ask becomes the retail price depends on how much stock reaches shelves in the final week.

The Courts Decide the Market

Unusually for a price story, the decisive variable sits in courtrooms. A single judge of the Madras High Court ruled on October 10 that only green crackers may be sold in Delhi, a restriction a division bench upheld; the Supreme Court heard the challenges and reserved its judgment on October 14. Every day without a final ruling is a day Sivakasi stock cannot move into India's largest Diwali market with certainty — and uncertainty, in a five-day selling season, is priced in.

The legal patchwork is widening beyond Delhi. In Mumbai, the Bombay High Court this week made its ban on bursting firecrackers on roads year-round, extending restrictions that used to be a Diwali-season argument into a permanent rule.

What Buyers Should Expect

For families buying this week: expect to pay at least 10% more than last Diwali at retail in the south, and considerably more in Delhi if green-cracker-only rules hold and supply stays thin. The gap between wholesale asks and retail tags should narrow — one way or the other — the moment the Supreme Court speaks. For Sivakasi's workers, the stakes are larger than a price chart: a weak season against ₹6,000 crore of unsold stock is the kind of year that closes small units for good.
